analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000 to extend the program's solvency.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to tax high earners' wages for Social Security won support from 12 senators but died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Social Security taxes stop applying to wages after a yearly cap. This bill would also tax wages above $250,000 per year, so the highest earners would keep paying into the program on income above that amount. The added revenue would help keep Social Security's trust fund from running short. The bill never got past the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who relies on Social Security, including current and future retirees, disabled workers, and survivors, because the extra tax revenue strengthens the program's finances. Workers in general also benefit indirectly, since a better-funded program is less likely to face future benefit cuts or a pushed-back retirement age.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security recipients and future retirees

how_it_helps.text: The bill would apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment earnings above $250,000 per year, in addition to the wages now taxed up to the annual cap, according to the CRS summary and bill text [S2][S3].
The extra revenue would flow into Social Security, helping close the program's long-term funding gap without cutting benefits or raising the retirement age [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The highest earners. Employees and self-employed people making more than $250,000 a year would pay the 12.4% combined tax on all income above that amount, and employers of highly paid workers would pay their half as well. Wages between the current cap (about $113,700 in 2013) and $250,000 would remain untaxed, a gap in the middle that leaves a steep jump at the $250,000 line.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers earning over $250,000 and their employers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a "donut hole": wages between the yearly cap and $250,000 would stay untaxed, so someone earning $240,000 pays nothing more while someone earning $260,000 pays on the excess — a sharp cliff at the $250,000 line that is hard to defend as fair [S3].

The bill raises taxes on high earners without increasing their Social Security benefits, breaking the usual link between what people pay in and what they get out; supporters see that as the wealthy paying their share, critics see it as turning Social Security further into a welfare program [S2][S3].

Payroll taxes are split with employers, so businesses that employ highly paid executives would face new costs on income above $250,000, which could pressure them to restructure pay or reduce other compensation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: Social Security is a universal program and closing its funding gap protects everyone's benefits. The cost falls on a small group — the roughly top few percent of earners — though the donut-hole design and the lack of any added benefit for those paying more are genuine design flaws an honest supporter would acknowledge. On balance the trade is heavily in favor of the majority, which is likely why opponents preferred the bill simply never come up rather than argue against it on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 7, 2013, joined by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and six other Democratic senators as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — the committee that writes tax law [S5].
No further action of any kind is recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
Eleven Democratic senators eventually cosponsored, but no Republican did, and the bill never came to a vote in the committee or on the floor before the Congress ended in January 2015 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The highest earners keep paying Social Security tax only up to the annual cap, and the trust fund gap remains unaddressed. Lawmakers who opposed the change are better off in that they never had to vote on it on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and the Finance Committee's inaction

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply Social Security payroll taxes above $250,000 and sought cosponsors.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original sponsor but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

for.name: 11 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Leahy, Boxer, Klobuchar, Whitehouse, Franken, and Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a dozen sponsors total.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it dead in committee.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no support for the bill; none cosponsored and the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican ever cosponsored, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee also declined to move it.

industries.note: Households earning more than $250,000 a year would pay Social Security tax on income above that level, with no increase in their own benefits. Because their gain from the status quo is the funding gap everyone else faces, their interest runs against the program's solvency for ordinary workers.

industries.industry: Employers of highly paid executives and professionals
industries.note: Employers pay a matching payroll tax share, so firms with highly compensated staff would owe more on wages above $250,000. This cost is small relative to most business taxes but concentrated in finance, law, and executive-heavy industries.
